implementation_notes: Separate Essence class holds compulsory properties and validates before calling CreationTarget constructor. CreationTarget constructors are restricted (private/friend or package-private). Essence passes itself to CreationTarget constructor so values can be retrieved. Clients must use Essence to create instances. Optional fluent interface on Essence for chaining setters. validateParameters() can be called at any time for early feedback.
code_sketch:
class ContractEssence
    _customer = None
    _supplier = None
    _start_date = None

    set_customer(cust) -> self
    set_supplier(supp) -> self
    set_start_date(date) -> self
    validate_parameters() -> bool
    create_contract() -> Contract

class Contract
    _customer
    _supplier
    _start_date

    constructor(essence: ContractEssence)

# Client usage:
essence = ContractEssence()
essence.set_customer(c).set_supplier(s).set_start_date(d)
contract = essence.create_contract()
pitfalls: Bypassing Essence: if clients can directly instantiate CreationTarget, the pattern provides no protection. Restrict constructor access carefully.
Inconsistent validation: validation logic split between Essence and CreationTarget can diverge, creating objects that pass creation but fail later use.
Temporal coupling: the Essence must be kept alive and in sync until createTarget() is called; premature modification or discard leads to invalid objects.
Incomplete validation: validating only at creation time ignores runtime state changes that can invalidate objects.
Excessive Essence coupling: creating separate Essence classes for every CreationTarget leads to class explosion; use generically typed Essence when appropriate.
Missing null handling: failing to handle null Essence or null property values in CreationTarget constructor causes cryptic errors.

Partially initialized entities from repositories or factories: returning entities with only a subset of properties loaded for performance reasons breaks invariants and allows invalid state transitions. Use DTOs for partial data; always return fully-initialized domain entities.

Using Specification pattern to validate new object creation: requires instantiating the object first in an invalid state, violating Always-Valid principles. Specifications should only validate already-existing domain objects.

Context-dependent validation confused with invariants: some validations appear context-dependent (e.g., field required on update but not on historical data load), but these are input-filtering concerns at the application boundary, not domain invariants.
Temporal coupling between Essence and CreationTarget: if the Essence is modified or discarded before createTarget() is called, the resulting object may be in an unintended state.

Wrong move: encoding compulsory properties as wire-format required fields (proto2 required) -> adding, removing, or renaming a required field breaks parse compatibility between old and new binaries, which is why Google banned the practice and proto3 removed required entirely -> instead keep the schema presence-friendly (optional with explicit presence tracking) and enforce compulsoriness at the Essence/application boundary, not on the wire.

Wrong move: relying solely on a runtime exception from build() (IllegalStateException in Immutables, UninitializedMessageException in protobuf Java) to guarantee validity -> missing-attribute failures surface in production at the first call that builds the object -> instead add compile-time enforcement such as staged/step builders (e.g., Immutables Style(stagedBuilder = true)), keeping the runtime check only as a backstop.

Wrong move: funneling every business rule through the Essence and CreationTarget constructor -> long unreadable creation protocols, entities forced to carry not-yet-available values, exception-driven control flow for ordinary user feedback, and context-dependent rules (valid-to-exist vs. valid-to-publish) hardcoded into the domain -> instead keep only the small set of true core invariants in the domain object and validate contextual rules at the application boundary or in specifications.
sources: Dombiak, Gaston & Prieto, Maximo. Design For Maintenance — OOPSLA 99 Position Paper — http://mcbreen.ab.ca/oopsla99/GastonDombiak.html
Gamma et al. Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software (1994) — Abstract Factory reference
Stroustrup, Bjarne. The Design and Evolution of C++ (1994) — inspiration for Essence pattern
